newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks fall sharply, close at year low.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks fall sharply, close at year low.

text.p: Tokyo stocks tumbled to their lowest level in a year on Thursday, battered by deepening gloom about Japan's economic outlook.
The stock market's benchmark Nikkei average slipped a steep 2.6 percent, its third biggest drop this year, on accelerated selling after sinking through key psychological levels.
"Market sentiment was feeble to begin with as there are too many uncertainties surrounding the economy," said Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities general manager.

The Nikkei dipped below the 20,000 level during the morning and fell through another key floor at around 19,920 points before settling 522.36 points down at 19,570.67, its lowest close since December 21 last year.
Brokers cited growing worries about the Japanese economy, which is still struggling to reach full recovery despite low interest rates and the prop of public spending.

In recent weeks, the Tokyo stock market has also been dragged down by a weaker Wall Street and general anxiety after a warning by U.S. Federal Reserve Board chairman Alan Greenspan about harmful "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.
Greenspan's remarks were seen as a signal that the United States might raise interest rates to curb the markets' zeal, which would have a knock-on effect on Japanese markets.

On December 6, after Greenspan's comments, the Nikkei posted its steepest single-day plunge of the year, shedding 667.20 points by the close. The index has lost 8.6 percent in little more than three weeks.
Thursday's renewed slump defied a modest rebound in the Dow overnight and relatively upbeat comments on the Japanese economy the day before from the Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor.
"Investors are highly sceptical about Japan's economic health and they think that the BOJ is just trying to boost sagging morale," one broker said.
On Wednesday, Japan's government issued a relatively modest forecast for economic growth in the next fiscal year but said the nation's recovery should continue.
Brokers said the succession of poor performances by Tokyo stocks in recent weeks had compounded the feeling of gloom.

Hideaki Akimoto, director and chief strategist at Daiwa Institute of Research, said that worries over the economic impact of a consumption tax hike next spring and the suspension of special income tax cuts were hanging over the market.
"Recent economic data, which is what the government bases its outlooks on, is showing slight signs of recovery but the momentum is probably not going to last," he said.
Public works spending is also due to be pared back, and there is concern about whether private spending can take its place as an engine of recovery.

"The market is starting to digest the bleak phase of the economy that is looming ahead," said Shinichi Ichikawa, strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities. "The factoring-in just started earlier than was initially expected."
After the Nikkei fell through the technical support levels, market participants began to feel that the index should fall as far as it wants, until the only way left to go is up, Nikko's Ueki added.
The Nikkei set a one-year intraday low of 19,560.39 before managing a light bounce near the close.
